title: Area II review: Preflight Procedures
intro: These questions mix the five ASEL Tasks of Area II: preflight assessment, flight deck management, engine starting, taxiing and the before-takeoff check. Many join two of them on one commercial flight, from the records check to the takeoff clearance.

questions.q: Your tour airplane's 100-hour inspection comes due at 2,310.0 hours. At 2,309.4 you start a 1.7-hour flight, with only crew aboard, to a shop that will do the 100-hour, using the 10-hour allowance for flying to an inspection. It lands at 2,311.1 and gets the inspection. When is the next 100-hour due?
options: 2,411.1 hours
2,409.4 hours
2,410.0 hours
2,420.0 hours
questions.why: The 100-hour limit may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours while en route to a place where the inspection can be done, and that excess time must be counted in the next 100 hours [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]] [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Excess: 2,311.1 - 2,310.0 = 1.1 hours. Next due: 2,311.1 + 100 - 1.1 = 2,410.0. 2,411.1 forgets to count the excess, and 2,420.0 treats the 10 hours as a bonus instead of an allowance for getting to the inspection.

questions.q: A customer books a paid photo flight along a coastline, on a clear day. Part of the route is over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore. Under 14 CFR 91.205, what must be aboard?
options: Flotation gear readily available to each occupant, plus a pyrotechnic signaling device
Flotation gear for the pilot only, since passengers are not crew, and a handheld radio
Nothing extra in daylight, because the over-water rule applies only to night flights
A life raft for the group, but only when the flight is flown under Part 135 rules
questions.why: For a flight for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore, 91.205(b)(12) requires approved flotation gear readily available to each occupant and, unless operating under Part 121, at least one pyrotechnic signaling device [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. It is in the VFR day list, paragraph (b), so it applies in daylight too; the night list is paragraph (c) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]]. The rule says each occupant, so pilot-only flotation does not meet it. The same route flown not for hire would not trigger this item.

questions.q: Your tour airplane has an airworthiness directive that requires a repetitive inspection every 50 hours of time in service. It comes due in 0.4 hours, and your next paid tour lasts 1.0 hour. The annual and 100-hour are both current. What is true?
options: You may fly the tour, because ADs allow up to 10 hours over, like the 100-hour
You may fly it if you log the 0.6 hour overrun in the maintenance records afterward
ADs are advisory for Part 91 airplanes, so the owner decides whether to comply
No. An AD's hour limit can't be passed unless the AD allows it; inspect first
questions.why: ADs are regulatory and must be complied with unless a specific exemption is granted. The PHAK uses this very case, a repetitive inspection every 50 hours, and says there is no provision to overfly an AD's maximum hour requirement unless it is written into the AD [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. The 10-hour allowance belongs only to the 100-hour inspection, and only while en route to where it can be done [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]], so it does not stretch an AD.

questions.q: Checking the records before a charter, you see the ELT transmitter has run for a total of about 70 minutes, from several accidental activations, since its battery was installed. The battery is at 30 percent of its useful life. What does the PHAK say?
options: Nothing yet, because replacement is due only at 50 percent of useful life
Replace or recharge the battery: total use is now over 1 cumulative hour
Nothing yet, because only a single unbroken run of more than an hour counts
Replace the whole ELT, because more than an hour of use means the unit has failed
questions.why: ELT batteries must be replaced, or recharged if rechargeable, when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50 percent of the battery's useful life has expired [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Either trigger is enough. 70 minutes of total use is more than 60, so the 30 percent useful life does not save it. The rule is about cumulative use, not one continuous run, and it calls for a battery, not a new ELT.

questions.q: Use the figure. For a paid tour you list two hazards: (1) flying through a line of thunderstorms, rated probable and catastrophic; (2) landing on a runway that is just long enough, rated occasional and critical. How does the matrix rate them, and what does the RMH say?
options: (1) high (red), (2) serious (yellow); both no-go until mitigated to medium or low
(1) serious (yellow), (2) high (red); both no-go until mitigated to medium or low
(1) high (red), (2) medium (green); fly, and mitigate only the runway if you can
Both medium (green); go, but mitigate both risks if you can
questions.why: Probable with catastrophic is high (red), and occasional with critical is serious (yellow); the RMH uses both as its examples [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. High or serious means no-go unless you find a way to reduce the risk so the next assessment shows medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. The second choice swaps the two ratings, and the last two rate the runway or the storms too low. Medium (green) is the only level that implies a go decision [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. If you are unsure between two levels, use the more conservative one [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

questions.q: Before an IFR charter you set the current altimeter setting. Field elevation is 1,240 ft and the altimeter reads 1,330 ft. What do you conclude?
options: It is fine, because it is within 100 ft of field elevation
It is fine; you can zero it yourself with a small screwdriver, as you would a VSI
It only matters above 18,000 ft, where everyone sets 29.92
It is 90 ft off, more than the 75 ft the AFH allows, so it is not acceptable for IFR
questions.why: Set to the current altimeter setting, the altimeter should read field elevation within 75 feet for IFR flight [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. 1,330 - 1,240 = 90 ft, which is outside that. The mechanical VSI is the only flight instrument the pilot may adjust; others need an FAA-certificated repairman or mechanic [[24:42|AFH 2-5]]. There is no 100 ft allowance in the AFH.

questions.q: A parent on your Part 91 tour brings a booster seat for her 5-year-old. It has no marking showing FAA approval. What is the rule?
options: Use it if it is secured to a forward-facing seat with the airplane's own seat belt
Use it only if the parent also holds the child on her lap the whole time
It is not approved for aircraft use; the child needs an approved seat and its own belt
Use it if it carries a motor vehicle safety standard label, since that is close enough
questions.why: Booster-type child restraints, along with vest- and harness-type ones, are not approved for use in aircraft unless they carry FAA approval markings [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)(B)(4)]]. So the child uses an approved seat with the belt secured during surface movement, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. A lap hold is only for a child who has not reached the second birthday and uses no restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]. A motor vehicle label alone does not override the booster exclusion.

questions.q: Taxiing to the run-up area on a paid tour, you notice a back-seat passenger has unbuckled to reach a camera bag. What do the rules say?
options: Everyone must be belted while taxiing, so have the passenger buckle up
It is allowed, because belts are required only for takeoff and landing
It is allowed at a nontowered airport, where the rule does not apply
Only front-seat occupants must stay belted while the airplane is taxiing
questions.why: Each person on board must occupy an approved seat with the safety belt, and shoulder harness if installed, secured during movement on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. Before moving on the surface you, the PIC, must make sure each person was told to fasten it [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]]. The rule covers every seat and every airport.

questions.q: Your new employer's SOP says: "Run the Before Takeoff checklist sometime during taxi, when convenient." What weakness does AC 120-71B point out?
options: No weakness; flexible timing lowers workload and keeps the pilot free to taxi
It is a floating start: tie it to a clear cue, such as a set point before the hold-short line
Checklists are better done from memory once a crew is experienced and comfortable
The checklist should wait until after the takeoff clearance is received from tower
questions.why: AC 120-71B says a checklist start is best anchored to a clear cue, such as reaching a point 2,000 feet before the hold-short line. "Floating" starts, left open to any time during taxi, create a high risk of starting late and rushing, or not starting at all [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.5]]. Doing a checklist while taxiing is itself high risk, because you can't give full attention to both [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.3]]. For one pilot, AC 91-73B adds: run checklists stopped, or taxiing straight with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]]. Flexible timing feels easier, but it is the trap.

questions.q: You fly a company single with a second pilot as pilot monitoring. Ground has cleared you to the runway. The PM wants to read the Before Takeoff checklist while you taxi, and you want to load the departure into the GPS at the same time. What fits FAA guidance?
options: Only one pilot head-down at a time: GPS while stopped, checklist stopped or on a straight taxiway
Do both at once while taxiing slowly, so the GPS and the checklist are done by the hold line
You, the taxiing pilot, read the checklist aloud while the PM watches outside the airplane
Skip the checklist, because the flow you already did before taxi is enough to go on
questions.why: With two pilots, only one should be head-down at any time the airplane is in motion [[59:19|AC 120-71B 5.2.2.1]]. GPS entries belong before the first taxi [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]], and pre-departure checklists are best done stopped or taxiing straight ahead with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]]. A flow does not replace the checklist: you do the flow, then use the checklist to confirm it [[59:17|AC 120-71B 5.1.2]]. Having the taxiing pilot read puts the wrong person head-down.

questions.q: Climbing on autopilot to an assigned 6,000 ft, you armed altitude capture. Passing 6,100 ft, the mode annunciator still shows vertical speed active, with the altitude mode only armed. What do the sources say?
options: Nothing is wrong; an armed mode always engages by itself, so keep monitoring
Reprogram the flight plan first, then deal with the altitude once that is done
It did not capture, so act now: select altitude hold or hand fly back to 6,000 ft
Wait; an armed mode often captures a few hundred feet late, so no action yet
questions.why: Managing the autopilot means knowing which modes are engaged and which are armed, verifying that armed functions such as altitude capture engage at the right time, and acting promptly when the system does not do what you expect [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. The annunciator is the source for who is doing what, and armed-to-active changes can hide an error until later [[59:29|AC 120-71B 6.9.1.1]] [[59:29|AC 120-71B 6.9.2]]. Reprogramming first leaves the path uncontrolled; a lower level of automation keeps the flight path in hand while you sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

questions.q: After the last tour of the night you shut the engine down, turn off the avionics and the master, and step out to help the passengers, leaving the ignition key on BOTH. A line worker starts to push the airplane back by its propeller. What is the hazard?
options: None, because with the master off there is no power for the spark plugs
Only the starter could engage, and it needs the key in START and the master on
The battery could slowly drain through the magnetos while the key is on
The engine can fire when the propeller moves; magnetos need no outside power
questions.why: After shutdown, turn the ignition switch OFF. Even with the battery and master switches OFF, the engine can fire and turn over if the ignition is left ON and the propeller is moved, because the magneto needs no outside source of electrical power [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. Magnetos are completely independent of the airplane's electrical system [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]], so the master switch protects no one. Whenever anyone touches a propeller, assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Your assessment lasts until the airplane is secured [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

questions.q: Your older airplane has a generator, not an alternator. Right after start, at 1,000 rpm with the lights and radios on, the ammeter sits a little on the minus side. At run-up rpm it moves to the plus side. What does this show?
options: A failing generator, so you should cancel the flight and call a mechanic
A voltage regulator failure that needs maintenance before flight
Normal: at low rpm a generator may not carry the full load, so the battery helps
A starter still engaged after the start, so shut the engine down
questions.why: Most DC generators don't make enough current at low engine rpm to run the whole electrical system, so the battery carries the load and can be drained quickly [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. On the ammeter, minus means more current drawn than replaced, and plus shows the battery charging. A full-scale minus deflection would mean a generator malfunction, and full-scale plus a regulator problem [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. A stuck starter shows as a high ammeter or loadmeter reading, low voltage, dim lights or radio noise [[18:1|AC 91-55A para 6]], not a small minus that clears with rpm.

questions.q: At the run-up, switching from BOTH to RIGHT gives no rpm drop at all, while LEFT gives a normal small drop. While you wait for a mechanic, a line worker wants to turn the propeller by hand to move the airplane. What is true?
options: No drop means the right magneto is working perfectly, so you may go flying
Not normal, so don't fly; and treat the propeller as live whenever anyone touches it
Don't fly, but the propeller is safe to move by hand once the key is turned OFF
Recheck at full throttle, and if there is still no drop the check has passed
questions.why: A small drop on each magneto is normal; the PHAK says no drop is not normal and the airplane should not be flown [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. Turning the key OFF does not make the propeller safe. A faulty switch can sit at OFF and still let the engine start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], and a broken magneto ground wire can let it start when the propeller is moved [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. So always assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: On a mild morning you start the engine for a paid tour with passengers belted in, and set about 1,000 rpm. Thirty-five seconds after the start the oil pressure gauge still reads zero, and a passenger asks if you are ready to go. What do you do?
options: Raise the rpm to 1,500 to build the pressure up, then taxi to the run-up area
Taxi to the run-up area, where the engine will warm up and the pressure will come
Shut the engine down and find the cause; oil pressure should show within 30 seconds
Wait another minute or two, because oil is often slow to reach the gauge on a start
questions.why: Check the oil pressure right after the start. If it does not show within 30 seconds, stop the engine and find the trouble [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. In most conditions it should reach at least the lower limit within 30 seconds, and if the limits are not reached, serious internal engine damage is likely [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. At 35 seconds you are past the limit, so more rpm, a longer wait or taxiing on only risks the engine. A passenger waiting does not change that; you are the final authority [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

questions.q: Your tour airplane was started with the wheels chocked. The engine is idling at warm-up rpm and a line worker must pull the chocks so you can taxi. What is the safe way?
options: Throttle to idle, and the worker reaches the chocks only from behind the propeller
Throttle to idle, and the worker comes from the front so you can see them
Leave warm-up rpm so the engine keeps cooling, and the worker comes in from the side, clear of the blade tips
Switch to one magneto to cut the power, and then any approach is safe
questions.why: The propeller is nearly invisible, and people have been seriously hurt or killed walking or reaching into its arc to pull chocks. Before the chocks are removed, set the throttle to idle and approach them only from the rear of the propeller, never from the front or the side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. One magneto still fires, and anyone touching a propeller should assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: You plan a night tour from a field with two runways. Which statement about a temporarily closed runway is true?
options: Yellow crosses mark each end only, and there may be no sign at all; check NOTAMs and ATIS
It always has lighted yellow crosses at both ends, so you can find out when you get there
White crosses are painted every 1,000 ft along the whole length of the closed runway
Its edge lights are turned off, which is the only sign that is ever used
questions.why: A temporarily closed runway has yellow crosses only at each end, or a raised lighted yellow cross may be used instead. But a visual sign may not be present at all, depending on the closure and the airport, so pilots should check NOTAMs and ATIS [[33:161|AIM 2-3-6e]]. That is why the PAVE environment check includes NOTAMs for closed runways and lights out [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]. A lighted cross is only one option, not a promise, so waiting to see it on arrival is the trap.

questions.q: Leaving the FBO ramp at a towered airport, you reach two yellow lines across the pavement: one solid, on your side, and one dashed, on the far side. What does this marking mean?
options: A runway holding position; stop and hold there until you are cleared onto the runway
A taxiway holding position; stop before it only when told to hold short
A taxiway edge; the pavement beyond it is not meant for aircraft
The movement area boundary; past the dashed line ATC controls you, so get a clearance
questions.why: The nonmovement area boundary is one solid and one dashed yellow line. The solid line is on the nonmovement side and the dashed line on the movement area side, the area under ATC [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]]. At an airport with an operating tower you need a clearance to operate on a taxiway [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]]. A runway holding position marking has four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]], and a taxiway/taxiway hold is a single dashed line [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5c]].

questions.q: Ground clears you to Runway 27 via Alpha. Your numbers show you could depart from the Alpha 3 intersection, halfway down, but you did not ask ground for it. What is expected?
options: Taxi on to Alpha 3 and line up there, since your numbers show it works
Hold short at Alpha 3 and call tower, since intersections need no approval
Taxi to, but not onto, the runway end; get ground's approval first if you want Alpha 3
Ask tower for the distance from Alpha 3 to the ends of the declared distances
questions.why: An aircraft is expected to taxi to, but not onto, the end of the assigned runway unless ground control approved an intersection departure, and you should state your position when calling the tower from an intersection [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10d]] [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10e]]. Before accepting one, your required takeoff distance must fit the reduced runway length and reduced declared distances [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]]. Controllers give the distance to the runway end on request, but they cannot give the distance to the ends of the declared distances [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10c]].

questions.q: Arriving on a paid flight in light rain, with a 2,500 ft ceiling and 5 miles visibility, Tower says: "Cleared to land Runway 27, hold short of Runway 36." The ALD looks just long enough for a dry runway. What fits the sources?
options: Accept, because the weather is well above the 1,000 ft and 3 mile LAHSO minimum
Decline and ask for full length; the PHAK says LAHSO is not authorized on wet runways
Accept, then use the whole runway anyway if the landing runs long
Accept with "wilco" and make the stop-or-continue decision during the rollout
questions.why: The PHAK lists LAHSO as not authorized on wet runways [[1:345|PHAK 14-11]]. That limit comes from the PHAK list only; AIM 4-3-11 does not state it. The answer is still the same under the AIM: the PIC has final authority to accept or decline and is expected to decline if it would compromise safety [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11b3]], and an ALD that only just fits a dry runway is not safe on a wet one. Once accepted, a LAHSO clearance must be followed unless amended or in an emergency, though you may still go around [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11b5]], so accepting now and using the full runway later is not an option. The 1,000 ft and 3 mile minimum is only the weather ATC needs to offer it [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11c5]], not proof that it fits your airplane.

questions.q: Taxiing in thick fog at a large airport, you become unsure whether you have passed your turn onto Taxiway Kilo. You can't see the tower. What does the AIM say?
options: Keep going slowly; the tower is watching and will warn you if you stray
Tell the controller at once, since the tower may not be able to see you
Turn onto the next taxiway that looks right, then confirm with the diagram
Run the Before Takeoff checklist now, while you work out where you are
questions.why: In low visibility the tower may not be able to see aircraft on the airport, so no one may be confirming you follow your instructions. Notify the controller at the first sign of becoming disoriented [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19a]] [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19b]]. Checklists and nonessential talk wait until you are stopped with the brakes set [[33:262|AIM 4-3-19d]]. You can also ask for progressive taxi [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18b3]]. Picking the taxiway that looks right is expectation bias at work [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

questions.q: Tower offers an intersection departure from Alpha 3 on Runway 9, which leaves 2,100 ft of runway ahead of you. The wind is a 6-knot tailwind, your lift-off speed is 60 knots, and the POH zero-wind takeoff distance is 1,800 ft. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, what should you do?
options: Accept, because the POH distance of 1,800 ft fits easily inside the 2,100 ft left
Accept, because 10 percent more for the tailwind is 1,980 ft, which still fits
Decline and ask for full length or another runway; you need about 2,180 ft
Accept, because a 6-knot tailwind is too light to change the distance much
questions.why: 6 / 60 = 10 percent of takeoff speed. A tailwind of 10 percent of takeoff airspeed increases takeoff distance about 21 percent [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]: 1,800 x 1.21 = 2,178, about 2,180 ft, which is more than the 2,100 ft left. The reduced runway length must still cover the distance you need before you accept an intersection [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]], and if you prefer the full length you are expected to tell ATC [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10a]]. 1,980 ft is a plain 10 percent guess, not the PHAK figure. You must know the runway lengths and takeoff distance data before every flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

questions.q: In a light single (a small aircraft) you are holding at an intersection 2,000 ft down Runway 27. A Boeing 757 has just taken off from the runway end. You would like to go right away. What applies?
options: Request a waiver of the 3-minute interval, and ATC can then clear you right away
No interval applies, because a 757 is large but not classed as a heavy
A 2-minute wait is enough, the same as after a larger aircraft's low approach
The 3-minute interval is mandatory for a small airplane behind a B757; you wait
questions.why: The waiver in AIM 4-3-10f is for a small aircraft behind a large nonheavy aircraft, and that paragraph leaves the B757 out [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10f]]. For small aircraft behind a B757 the 3-minute interval is mandatory [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10h]]. The 500 foot exception does not help, because you are 2,000 ft down the runway [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10g]]. The 2-minute wait is for a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]]. When you do go, rotate before the 757's rotation point and climb above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b6]].

questions.q: At the run-up spot on a cool morning, the oil temperature is still below the POH minimum for takeoff power, and the cylinder head temperature is in its normal range. What fits the AFH?
options: Close the cowl flaps so the engine warms up faster, then depart as normal once it feels ready
Take off now with takeoff power, because the oil warms up quickly once you are in the climb
Nose into wind, cowl flaps open, watch CHT, and no takeoff power until oil reaches minimum
Hold high power on the ground until the oil temperature finally comes up to minimum
questions.why: Many engines need a minimum oil temperature before takeoff power, so verify it before applying high power [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Prolonged ground running can overheat the cylinders long before oil temperature rises, so head into the wind and watch the cylinder head temperature [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Cowl flaps stay open on the ground and are never closed for warm-up [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Full power while waiting is the overheating risk, and taking off cold skips the POH check.

questions.q: Before takeoff in an airplane with electric trim and an autopilot, which check fits the AFH?
options: Cycle the trim both ways, check the disconnect, set takeoff trim, and finish autopilot checks first
Engage the autopilot first, then let it run its own self-test once airborne
Check only that the trim indicator shows takeoff, since testing the switch could cause a runaway
Skip the disconnect check, because a trim circuit breaker that is in covers any trim problem
questions.why: The AFH has you actuate the trim switch both ways, verify the trim disconnect (if equipped) works, then set takeoff trim [[24:344|AFH 17-10]]. All flight director and autopilot computer and trim checks come before engagement, and many systems need a self-test first [[24:257|AFH 13-8]]. For a trim runaway you press the disconnect or pull the trim circuit breaker [[24:348|AFH 17-14]], so you need to know both work and where they are. A breaker that is in tells you nothing about the disconnect.
